name: CrackMapExec - Find Logged-On Users
description: Enumerates users currently logged on to target hosts via the NetWkstaUserEnum RPC call. High-value intelligence: find where Domain Admins, IT staff, or privileged accounts have active sessions. Enables targeted lateral movement — compromise the machine where the DA is logged in → get DA token.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== WHY LOGGED-ON USERS MATTERS ===
In token-based attacks (PTH, impersonation), you need to target machines where
high-privilege users have ACTIVE sessions:
  - DA logged into WS01 → compromise WS01 → steal DA token
  - Admin logged into file server → pivot there, impersonate
  - Service account running on server → dump LSASS → get hash

BloodHound also shows this via 'HasSession' edges (requires collection timing
to be right when DA is logged in).

=== OUTPUT ===
  SMB  172.16.5.25  445  ACADEMY-EA-MS01  INLANEFREIGHT\administrator  (Pwn3d!)
  SMB  172.16.5.25  445  ACADEMY-EA-MS01  INLANEFREIGHT\adunn

See 'administrator' logged in → target this machine for token theft.

=== SWEEP SUBNET FOR SESSION HUNTING ===
crackmapexec smb 172.16.5.0/23 -u forend -p Klmcargo2 --loggedon-users | grep 'administrator\|admin\|DA'

=== SHARPHOUND ALTERNATIVE ===
SharpHound (-c Session) collects session data and shows it in BloodHound.
BloodHound query: 'Find Active Domain Admin Sessions'

=== REQUIRES ADMIN ON TARGET ===
NetWkstaUserEnum requires local admin rights on the target machine.
For non-admin: try NetSessionEnum (less detailed but lower privilege requirement).

defense.why_it_works: The Windows service enumerating logged-on users (via SAMR/remote registry) returns sessions to any authenticated caller with access, revealing where privileged users are active for token/TGT theft.
defense.prerequisites: Local-admin credentials and SMB access to the hosts.
defense.impact: Where privileged users are logged in - targets for token theft/PtH.
defense.detection: SMB tree-connects and share/RID enumeration (Event 5140/5145 with share auditing); anonymous/null binds and RID cycling against the DC.
defense.prevention: AD is readable by any authenticated user by design, so prevention is limited - focus on DETECTION (Defender for Identity, LDAP/SMB anomaly monitoring), least privilege, disabling anonymous/null sessions, and REDUCING what's exposed (remove unnecessary SPNs, descriptions with secrets, over-shared folders).
defense.evasion: Use built-in tools (net, AD module, dsquery) that blend with normal admin activity; throttle and scope collection; avoid the noisiest methods (full BloodHound sweeps, RID brute) where Defender for Identity is present.
defense.misconfiguration: Active Directory's default read ACL allows any authenticated domain user to enumerate nearly the entire directory: all user accounts, groups, SPNs, computer objects, trust relationships, and many sensitive attributes. There is no built-in 'need to know' principle on LDAP reads. BloodHound, PowerView, and ldapsearch all exploit these open default ACLs to map attack paths.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# AD default permissions — authenticated users can read:
# All user objects: sAMAccountName, userPrincipalName, memberOf, servicePrincipalName
# All computer objects: DNS names, OS versions, operating system attributes
# All group memberships, GPOs, OU structure, domain trusts

# Verify with any low-priv account:
Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties *  # returns all users + attributes
Get-ADGroup -Filter * | Get-ADGroupMember  # all group memberships
defense.secure_config:
# 1. Enable AD Recycle Bin + Protected Users group
# 2. Audit and tighten ACLs on sensitive attributes:
#    msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo, adminCount, memberOf for privileged groups

# 3. Disable SMB null sessions + restrict LDAP anonymous binds (see smb/ldap cards)

# 4. Detect enumeration via volume:
# Sysmon Event 3 (network connection) from non-DC to DC on port 389/636
# Event 4661 — access to SAM objects (high-volume; baseline first)
# Microsoft Defender for Identity: 'Account Enumeration Reconnaissance' alert

# 5. Deploy Honey accounts/objects:
# Fake high-priv account (no real access) — any LDAP query for it = attacker
# BloodHound run from non-DC = detectable via DC LDAP traffic volume

# 6. Tiered administration: Tier 0 DCs, Tier 1 servers, Tier 2 workstations
#    Each tier can only query its own tier's objects
